chapters.name: Time, Speed & Distance
chapters.tagline: Rebuild the one relationship, then the four shapes it takes: units, relative speed, trains, boats.
chapters.intro: One relationship and the four shapes it takes: units, relative speed, trains, boats. Tap a concept to see it worked in detail, then work through 5 questions built around the traps that catch people out most.

overview_cards.headline: Speed = D / T
overview_cards.note:
**Why it works:** speed is just distance covered per unit time — rearrange the same relationship to solve for whichever quantity is missing.

- e.g. a car covers 150 km in 3 h → speed $=150/3=50$ km/h.
- For a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional: if speed becomes 3/4 of the original, time becomes 4/3.

overview_cards.headline: Total distance / total time
overview_cards.note:
**Why the plain average is wrong:** you spend more time travelling at the slower speed, so it pulls the true average toward itself — total distance over total time captures that automatically.

- e.g. 40 km/h then 60 km/h over two equal-distance legs: average $=\dfrac{2\times40\times60}{40+60}=48$ km/h, not the naive 50.
- **Equal-legs shortcut:** $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ — the harmonic mean of the two speeds.

**Why 5/18:** $1$ km/h $=\dfrac{1000\text{ m}}{3600\text{ s}}=\dfrac{5}{18}$ m/s — it falls straight out of unit cancellation.

- Anchors: **36 km/h = 10 m/s**, 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
- e.g. 90 km/h $\to 90\times5/18=25$ m/s.

**Why add or subtract:** moving toward each other, the gap closes at the combined rate; moving the same way, the faster one only pulls ahead at the *difference* in speeds.

- e.g. two cars at 40 and 60 km/h toward each other close the gap at $100$ km/h; the same two cars going the same way close it at just $20$ km/h.
- Drives every meeting, overtaking and crossing problem.

**Why the length gets added:** "crossing" means the front travels until the *back* of the train clears the obstacle — so the train's own length always joins whatever it's crossing.

- e.g. a 150 m train crossing a 100 m platform covers $150+100=250$ m in total, not just 150 m.

**Why add or subtract the stream:** it's just relative speed with the current as the second mover — the water helps you downstream and fights you upstream.

- e.g. boat speed 8 km/h, stream 2 km/h → downstream $=10$, upstream $=6$ km/h.
- Run the formulas in reverse to recover b and s from two measured travel speeds.

items.title: Relative speed
items.body:
- Opposite directions: add the speeds. Same direction: subtract.
- e.g. 40 & 60 km/h toward each other → 100 km/h combined.

items.title: Boats & streams
items.body:
- Downstream = boat + stream; upstream = boat − stream.
- e.g. boat 8, stream 2 → down 10, up 6.

items.title: Average speed
items.body:
- Total distance ÷ total time — never the plain average of the speeds.
- Equal-legs shortcut: $2ab/(a+b)$.

chapters.name: Number System
chapters.tagline: Standard form, the remainder relation, cyclicity, HCF/LCM — the toolkit behind most of quant.
chapters.intro: Number System is less a single topic than a toolkit: standard form, the remainder relation, cyclicity and HCF/LCM resurface everywhere else in quant. Read it top to bottom to rebuild the whole picture, then work through 14 real CAT questions, one per recurring pattern.

overview_cards.headline: I = QN + R
overview_cards.note:
**Why it works:** for any integer I and any positive N, there's exactly one way to split I into "N times something" plus a leftover between 0 and N−1 — that leftover is the remainder. Because it's unique, you can always trust R without re-deriving it.

- e.g. $23 = 5\times4+3$ — divide 23 by 5: quotient 4, remainder 3.
- e.g. a bigger one: $157 = 12\times13+1$ — quotient 13, remainder 1.
- Every divisibility, remainder and cyclicity question in this chapter reduces to this one relation.

overview_cards.headline: The true remainder is never negative
overview_cards.note:
**Why it happens:** the definition requires $0 \le R < N$, so when I is negative, the quotient must be pushed further down (more negative) until the remainder lands back inside that range — it can never spill below 0.

- e.g. $-25 \div 7$: $-25 = 7\times(-4)+3$, so the remainder is **3**, not $-4$.
- **Useful shortcut:** you can still *calculate* with the negative form mid-problem (e.g. treat $13 \div 8$ as remainder $-3$ instead of 5) — just convert back into $[0, N)$ by adding N at the very end.

**Why 1 isn't prime:** primality needs *exactly two* distinct divisors (1 and itself); 1 has only one divisor total, so it's excluded by definition. **Why 2 is the only even prime:** every other even number is divisible by 2 *and* itself, giving at least 3 divisors.

- e.g. is 91 prime? $\sqrt{91}\approx9.5\to z=10$; check 2, 3, 5, 7 — $91=7\times13$, so **not** prime.
- e.g. is 97 prime? check 2, 3, 5, 7 — none divide it, so 97 **is** prime.
- **Primality test:** round √N up to z, then check every prime ≤ z.
- **Primes 1–100:** 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 … 97 — 25 of them.

**Why the 99(c−a) always appears:** a 3-digit number is $100a+10b+c$; its reverse is $100c+10b+a$. Subtracting, the $10b$ term cancels completely, leaving $99(c-a)$ — the middle digit never affects this trick at all.

- e.g. 573 reversed is 375: $573-375=198=99\times2$, matching $a-c=5-3=2$.
- The 2-digit version works the same way: reverse − original for $10a+b$ is $9(b-a)$.

lines: "At least one …" → total − the clean complement
Build digit-by-digit: each new digit avoids the ones already used
overview_cards.note:
**Why count the complement:** counting "at least one repeat" directly means juggling many overlapping cases (a repeat in positions 1&2, or 1&3, or 2&3, or all three...). It's far simpler to count the clean case (no repeats at all) and subtract it from the total.

- e.g. 3-digit numbers with all-distinct digits: $9\times9\times8=648$ (first digit ≠ 0, each next digit avoids what's already taken).
- So "at least one repeated digit" $=900-648=252$.
- The same idea extends to any length: each new position just has one fewer available digit than the last.

lines: Sum of factors = (Σ powers of p₁)(Σ powers of p₂)…
overview_cards.note:
**Why the formula works:** a factor of $p_1^ap_2^b\ldots$ is built by independently picking a power of each prime — $0$ to $a$ for $p_1$ (that's $a+1$ choices), $0$ to $b$ for $p_2$, and so on. Multiplying the choice-counts together gives every possible factor exactly once.

- e.g. $40=2^3\cdot5^1 \Rightarrow (3+1)(1+1)=8$ factors; sum of factors $=(1+2+4+8)(1+5)=90$.
- e.g. perfect-square factors of 40: need even powers only $\Rightarrow 2^0$ or $2^2$ (2 choices) $\times\ 5^0$ (1 choice) $=2$ factors — namely 1 and 4.
- **Even factors:** drop the 2⁰ term (forces at least one 2). **Odd factors:** keep only 2⁰ (forbids every 2).

**Why the difference method works:** if x divides both n₁ and n₂, it must also divide their difference $n_1-n_2$ — so the HCF can never exceed that difference, which narrows the whole search down to just its factors.

- e.g. HCF(39, 78, 195): smallest difference $78-39=39$; factors of 39 are 1, 3, 13, 39 — test the largest first: 39 divides all three, so **HCF = 39**.
- e.g. HCF(150, 210, 375) via standard form $=15$; LCM (same numbers) $=5250$.
- The product rule (HCF × LCM = n₁ × n₂) only holds for exactly two numbers, not three or more.

lines: 0, 1, 5, 6 → always keep the same units digit
Every other digit cycles with period dividing 4
overview_cards.note:
**Why the cycle length divides 4:** a units digit only depends on repeatedly multiplying by itself, mod 10 — and mod 10, any digit's multiplicative pattern is forced to close back on itself within 4 steps.

- e.g. $7^{203}$: units digit of 7 cycles 7, 9, 3, 1; $203=4\times50+3 \Rightarrow$ 3rd in the cycle → **3**.
- e.g. $8^{203}$: units digit of 8 cycles 8, 4, 2, 6; same $203=4\times50+3 \Rightarrow$ 3rd in the cycle → **2**.
- Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 have a cycle length of 1 — they never change, however high the power.
- Any factorial ≥ 4! is a multiple of 4, so it always lands on the "4n" column.

rows.label: (aX − 1)ⁿ ÷ a
rows.value: +1 if n even, a−1 if n odd

overview_cards.note:
**Why it works:** expand $(aX+1)^n$ with the binomial theorem — every term except the very last carries a factor of $aX$, so it's divisible by $a$ and vanishes mod $a$; only the last term, $1^n=1$, survives. The $(aX-1)^n$ case is identical, except the surviving term is $(-1)^n$.

- e.g. $37^{12635} \div 9 \to 1$, since $37=9\times4+1$ — the $+1$ form, so the remainder is 1 regardless of the exponent.
- e.g. $31^{127} \div 8$: since $31=8\times4-1$, this is the $-1$ form with $n=127$ (odd) $\to (-1)^{127}=-1 \to$ remainder $8-1=7$.
- **General tactic:** if the base isn't already $\pm1$ away from a multiple of the divisor, find a power of it that is — e.g. mod 7: $2^3=8\equiv1$, so $2^{100}=2^{3\times33+1}\equiv2^1=2 \pmod7$.

rows.value: alt. digit sums differ by 0 or a multiple of 11

overview_cards.note:
**Why the digit-sum rules work (3, 9):** $10\equiv1\pmod9$, so every place value $10^k\equiv1$ too — meaning a number's value mod 9 is just the sum of its digits (and mod 3 works the same way). **Why 11 alternates:** $10\equiv-1\pmod{11}$, so place values alternate $+1,-1,+1,\ldots$, which is exactly the alternating digit sum.

- e.g. is 4983 divisible by 11? Alternating sum (right to left) $=3-8+9-4=0 \Rightarrow$ yes.
- 7, 11 and 13 share a test: split into 3-digit blocks from the right and alternately add/subtract, since $1001=7\times11\times13$.

lines: Power of prime p in n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + …
overview_cards.note:
**Why only count 5's for zeroes:** a trailing zero needs a 2 *and* a 5 paired up, and factorials always contain far more multiples of 2 than of 5 — so 5 is always the bottleneck. **Why take the minimum for a composite divisor:** the whole divisor can only appear as many times as its scarcest required prime allows.

- e.g. zeroes in $27! = \lfloor27/5\rfloor+\lfloor27/25\rfloor=5+1=6$.
- e.g. power of $42=2\cdot3\cdot7$ in $122!$: 7 is the scarcest of the three primes, so just count 7's — $\lfloor122/7\rfloor+\lfloor122/49\rfloor=17+2=19$.

overview_cards.headline: Aᵖ⁻¹ ÷ P → remainder 1
overview_cards.subheadline: when P is prime and P doesn't divide A
overview_cards.note:
**Why Fermat's theorem is true:** among $1, 2, \ldots, P-1$, multiplying every one of them by A (mod P) just re-shuffles the same set in a different order — so their product is unchanged mod P, which forces $A^{P-1}\equiv1$. **Why CRT helps:** solving two smaller, simpler congruences and recombining is far easier than wrestling with one large composite modulus directly.

- e.g. $2^{256}\div17=(2^4)^{64}=16^{64}\equiv(-1)^{64}=1$ — a Fermat-flavoured shortcut.
- e.g. CRT: $107^{1444}\div136$ (split $136=17\times8$) → mod 17 it's a "17n+13" number, mod 8 it's an "8n+1" number; the only value under 136 satisfying both at once is **81**.

items.title: Cyclicity
items.body:
- Units digit of $N^n$ repeats with a cycle that divides 4.
- Write $n = 4k+x$, then read the digit off N's own last digit and x.

items.title: Standard form factors
items.body:
- Factors of $p_1^a p_2^b \ldots$ = $(a+1)(b+1)\ldots$
- Perfect-square factors: keep only even powers in every bracket.

items.title: HCF & LCM
items.body:
- HCF × LCM = $n_1 \times n_2$ — valid for two numbers only.
- HCF of a set always divides every pairwise difference.

items.title: Large powers
items.body:
- $(aX+1)^n \div a \to$ remainder 1, always.
- $(aX-1)^n \div a \to$ +1 if n even, $a-1$ if n odd.

items.title: Negative remainders
items.body:
- $13 \div 8$ can be read as remainder 5, or as $-3$.
- Use whichever is smaller to calculate with, then convert back into $[0,N)$ at the end.

items.title: Legendre's formula
items.body:
- Power of prime p in $n!$ = $\lfloor n/p \rfloor + \lfloor n/p^2 \rfloor + \ldots$
- Zeroes in $n!$ = just the count of 5's — they're always scarcer than 2's.

items.title: Fermat's little theorem
items.body:
- If P is prime and $P \nmid A$: $A^{P-1} \div P$ leaves remainder 1.
- No shortcut for a composite modulus? Split into co-primes (CRT), solve each, recombine.

questions.question_text: Riya drives the first half of a trip at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Her average speed for the whole trip is:
questions.concept:
- "Average speed" always means total distance ÷ total time — never the plain average of the two speeds.
- For two equal-distance legs this collapses to the harmonic mean, $2ab/(a+b)$, which always sits below the plain average, pulled toward the slower speed.
questions.solution:
1. **Spot the trap:** the two legs cover equal distances, so this is not a plain average of 40 and 60.
2. **Apply the equal-legs formula:** average speed $=\dfrac{2\times40\times60}{40+60}=\dfrac{4800}{100}=48$ km/h.
3. **Sanity check:** 48 sits below the naive average of 50, since more time was spent at the slower 40 km/h — the bait answer.

questions.question_text: A 180 m long train crosses a pole in 12 seconds. Its speed is:
questions.concept:
- Crossing a pole/point means covering exactly the train's own length — no platform, no second train to add.
- Work out speed in m/s from the given data first, then convert to km/h (× 18/5) only at the end.
questions.solution:
1. **Identify the distance:** crossing a pole means covering just the train's own 180 m length.
2. **Compute speed in m/s:** $180\div12=15$ m/s.
3. **Convert to km/h:** $15\times18/5=54$ km/h.

questions.question_text: Two trains, 120 m and 180 m long, move toward each other at 40 km/h and 50 km/h. Time to completely cross each other?
questions.concept:
- Moving toward each other, relative speed = the sum of the two speeds; the distance to cover is the sum of both train lengths.
- Convert everything to the same unit (m/s or km/h) before combining.
questions.solution:
1. **Add the lengths:** combined distance to cover $=120+180=300$ m.
2. **Add the speeds (opposite directions):** $40+50=90$ km/h $=25$ m/s.
3. **Divide:** time $=300\div25=12$ s.

questions.question_text: A boat covers 24 km downstream in 3 hours. If the stream flows at 2 km/h, the boat’s speed in still water is:
questions.concept:
- Downstream speed = boat + stream; upstream = boat − stream — two equations, two unknowns.
- Given one direction's speed and the stream, isolate the boat's own speed by adding or subtracting the stream.
questions.solution:
1. **Find the downstream speed:** $24\text{ km}\div3\text{ h}=8$ km/h.
2. **Downstream = boat + stream:** $8=\text{boat}+2$.
3. **Solve for the boat:** boat speed $=8-2=6$ km/h.

questions.question_text: Walking at 5 km/h a man reaches office 6 min late; at 6 km/h he is 4 min early. The distance to his office is:
questions.concept:
- Two different speeds over the *same* distance give two different travel times — set up $\text{time}_1-\text{time}_2$ using $d/s$ for each.
- Convert the "late" and "early" minutes into a single total time gap before solving for distance.
questions.solution:
1. **Convert minutes to hours:** total time gap $=6+4=10$ min $=1/6$ h.
2. **Set up the equation:** at 5 km/h he's 6 min late, at 6 km/h he's 4 min early, so $\dfrac{d}{5}-\dfrac{d}{6}=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
3. **Simplify the left side:** $\dfrac{d}{30}=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
4. **Solve:** $d=5$ km.

questions.question_text: When $3^{333}$ is divided by 11, the remainder is
questions.concept:
- Powers of a number, taken mod some divisor, always start repeating — that repeating block is the **cycle**.
- Find it by listing successive powers mod the divisor until a value repeats.
- Reduce the exponent using $\text{exponent} \bmod \text{cycle length}$ — the leftover tells you which remainder in the cycle to read off.
questions.solution:
1. **Spot the cycle:** $3^1=3,\ 3^2=9,\ 3^3=27\equiv5,\ 3^4\equiv4,\ 3^5\equiv1 \pmod{11}$ — it repeats every 5 powers.
2. **Reduce the exponent:** $333 = 5\times66+3$, so only the leftover power of 3 matters.
3. **Read off the remainder:** $3^{333}\equiv3^3=27\equiv5\pmod{11}$.

*Source: CAT 2024, Slot 2.*

questions.question_text: When $10^{100}$ is divided by 7, the remainder is
questions.concept:
- A big or awkward base almost always simplifies first — reduce it mod the divisor before touching the exponent.
- Once the base is small, it's a plain cyclicity problem: list powers until the remainders repeat.
- With a **prime** divisor P, Fermat's little theorem guarantees the cycle length divides P−1.
questions.solution:
1. **Simplify the base:** $10\equiv3\pmod7$, so track powers of 3 instead of 10.
2. **Spot the cycle:** $3^n\pmod7$ repeats as $\{3,2,6,4,5,1\}$ — cycle length 6.
3. **Reduce the exponent:** $100=6\times16+4$, so only the leftover power of 4 matters.
4. **Read off the remainder:** $10^{100}\equiv3^4=81\equiv4\pmod7$.

*Source: CAT 2024, Slot 1.*

questions.question_text: The sum of digits of the number $(625)^{65}\times(128)^{36}$, is
questions.concept:
- Break every base down into its prime factors before doing anything else.
- Pair up matching 2's and 5's — each pair is one factor of 10, i.e. one trailing zero.
- Only the leftover, un-paired digits affect the actual digit sum; the zeroes contribute nothing.

questions.question_text: How many factors of $2^4\times3^5\times10^4$ are perfect squares which are greater than 1?
questions.concept:
- Reduce any mixed base (like 10, 12, 6) into pure prime factors before counting anything.
- A factor is a perfect square only if **every** prime in it has an even exponent.
- Count the even-exponent choices for each prime separately, then multiply the counts together.
- Watch for "greater than 1" conditions — they usually mean subtract the factor 1 at the end.
questions.solution:
1. **Reduce to prime form:** $2^4\times3^5\times10^4=2^4\times3^5\times2^4\times5^4=2^8\times3^5\times5^4$.
2. **Force even exponents (perfect squares):** $2^a3^b5^c$ needs $a\in\{0,2,4,6,8\}$ (5 choices), $b\in\{0,2,4\}$ (3), $c\in\{0,2,4\}$ (3).
3. **Multiply the choices:** $5\times3\times3=45$ perfect-square factors in total.
4. **Drop the factor 1:** the question wants squares greater than 1, so $45-1=44$.

*Source: CAT 2019, Slot 2.*

questions.question_text: The number of all natural numbers up to 1000 with non-repeating digits is
questions.concept:
- Split counting problems by number of digits (1-digit, 2-digit, 3-digit…) and add the totals at the end.
- For each position, count how many digits are still available given what's already been used.
- The leading digit of a multi-digit number can never be 0 — exclude it there, nowhere else.
- Check boundary values (like 1000 itself) separately; they often break a pattern that otherwise holds.
questions.solution:
1. **Split by digit count:** count 1-digit, 2-digit and 3-digit numbers separately.
2. **1-digit:** 1–9 → 9 numbers.
3. **2-digit:** 9 choices for the first digit × 9 for the second (any digit but the first) $=81$.
4. **3-digit:** $9\times9\times8=648$ (1000 itself repeats a digit, so it's excluded).
5. **Add them up:** $9+81+648=738$.

*Source: CAT 2023, Slot 1.*

questions.question_text: How many three-digit numbers are greater than 100 and increase by 198 when the three digits are arranged in the reverse order?
questions.concept:
- Represent an unknown number by its digits algebraically, e.g. $100a+10b+c$ for a 3-digit number.
- "Reverse minus original" (or vice versa) for a 3-digit number always collapses to a clean multiple of 99.
- Once you know the digit difference, count valid digit pairs, then multiply by the free choices for the untouched digit.
questions.solution:
1. **Set up the number:** let it be $100a+10b+c$.
2. **Use the reversal condition:** reversed − original $=198 \Rightarrow 99(c-a)=198 \Rightarrow c-a=2$.
3. **Count valid $(a,c)$ pairs:** (1,3),(2,4),(3,5),(4,6),(5,7),(6,8),(7,9) — 7 pairs.
4. **Count free choices for b:** any of 0–9, so 10 values.
5. **Multiply:** $7\times10=70$.

*Source: CAT 2021, Slot 1.*

questions.question_text: For a 4-digit number, the sum of its digits in the thousands, hundreds and tens places is 14, the sum of its digits in the hundreds, tens and units places is 15, and the tens place digit is 4 more than the units place digit. Then the highest possible 4-digit number satisfying the above conditions is
questions.concept:
- Name every digit as its own variable, then translate each sentence into one equation.
- Combine or subtract the equations to eliminate variables until everything is in terms of just one.
- To maximise (or minimise) a digit, push the remaining free variable to its largest (or smallest) value that still keeps every digit between 0 and 9.
questions.solution:
1. **Name the digits:** $a,b,c,d$ from left to right.
2. **Translate the clues:** $a+b+c=14$, $b+c+d=15$, and $c=d+4$.
3. **Simplify:** subtracting the first two clues gives $d=a+1$, so $c=d+4=a+5$.
4. **Substitute back:** $a+b+c=14 \Rightarrow 2a+b=9$.
5. **Maximise $a$:** the largest valid $a=4$, giving $b=1,\ c=9,\ d=5$ — all valid digits.
6. **Read off the number:** 4195.

*Source: CAT 2021, Slot 2.*

questions.question_text: How many integers in the set {100, 101, 102, …, 999} have at least one digit repeated?
questions.concept:
- "At least one repeat" is a signal to use the complement: total count minus the all-distinct-digits count.
- Counting the "no repeats" case is almost always the easier direction to build directly, digit by digit.
- Each new digit position just avoids whichever digits were already used in the earlier positions.
questions.solution:
1. **Total 3-digit numbers:** 900 (100 to 999).
2. **Count all-distinct-digit numbers:** $9\times9\times8=648$ (first digit ≠ 0, each next digit avoids the ones already used).
3. **Take the complement:** numbers with at least one repeat $=900-648=252$.

*Source: CAT 2020, Slot 3.*

questions.question_text: If the product of three consecutive positive integers is 15600 then the sum of the squares of these integers is
questions.concept:
- For a product of consecutive integers, estimate the middle value with a root — square root for two numbers, cube root for three, and so on.
- Round that estimate to the nearest integer and verify directly; consecutive-integer products pin down a single answer fast.
- Once the integers are known, the rest is just direct computation.
questions.solution:
1. **Estimate the integers:** $\sqrt[3]{15600}\approx25$, so try integers around 25.
2. **Check:** $24\times25\times26=15600$ ✓.
3. **Square and add:** $24^2+25^2+26^2=576+625+676$.
4. **Total:** $576+625+676=1877$.

*Source: CAT 2017, Slot 2.*

questions.question_text: How many two-digit numbers, with a non-zero digit in the units place, are there which are more than thrice the number formed by interchanging the positions of its digits?
questions.concept:
- Represent the two-digit number algebraically as $10a+b$, and its digit-swap as $10b+a$.
- Translate the comparison in words directly into an inequality between $a$ and $b$.
- Fix the smaller-range digit first (usually the units digit) and test each value — the valid range for the other digit narrows fast.
questions.solution:
1. **Set up the number:** let it be $10a+b$, with $b\ne0$.
2. **Translate the condition:** $10a+b>3(10b+a) \Rightarrow 7a>29b$.
3. **Try $b=1$:** $a>29/7\approx4.14 \Rightarrow a=5,6,7,8,9$ — numbers 51, 61, 71, 81, 91.
4. **Try $b=2$:** $7a>58 \Rightarrow a=9$ — number 92.
5. **Try $b\ge3$:** no valid $a\le9$ works.
6. **Count them all:** 51, 61, 71, 81, 91, 92 → 6 numbers.

*Source: CAT 2018, Slot 2.*

questions.question_text: A school has less than 5000 students and if the students are divided equally into teams of either 9 or 10 or 12 or 25 each, exactly 4 are always left out. However, if they are divided into teams of 11 each, no one is left out. The maximum number of teams of 12 each that can be formed out of the students in the school is
questions.concept:
- "Same remainder for several divisors" always translates to $N = \text{lcm(divisors)} \times k + \text{remainder}$.
- Bring in any leftover condition (like exact divisibility by one more number) to pin down which $k$ works.
- Use the upper bound given in the question to confirm you've found the right (and only) valid N.
questions.solution:
1. **Translate the remainder clue:** N leaves remainder 4 when divided by 9, 10, 12 or 25, so $N=\text{lcm}(9,10,12,25)\cdot k+4=900k+4$.
2. **Bring in the 11 clue:** N must also be exactly divisible by 11.
3. **Test small $k$:** at $k=2$, $N=1804=11\times164$ ✓, and $1804<5000$.
4. **Divide into teams of 12:** $1804=12\times150+4$, so the maximum full teams of 12 is $\lfloor1804/12\rfloor=150$.

*Source: CAT 2022, Slot 3.*

questions.question_text: The number of positive integers less than 50, having exactly two distinct factors other than 1 and itself, is
questions.concept:
- Translate "factors other than 1 and itself" into a total factor count by adding back those two.
- Recall which prime-power shapes give a specific factor count — e.g. exactly 4 factors means the number is $p^3$ or $p\cdot q$ for distinct primes.
- List the candidates for each shape separately within the given bound, then add the counts.
questions.solution:
1. **Decode the condition:** "exactly two distinct factors other than 1 and itself" means exactly 4 factors in total.
2. **Know the two shapes with 4 factors:** $p^3$ (since $3+1=4$) or $p\cdot q$ for distinct primes $p,q$ (since $2\times2=4$).
3. **Count the $p^3$ case below 50:** $2^3=8$, $3^3=27$ → 2 numbers.
4. **Count the $p\cdot q$ case below 50:** 6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, 26, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 46 → 13 numbers.
5. **Add them up:** $2+13=15$.

*Source: CAT 2023, Slot 2.*

questions.tag: Fixed divisors of a variable expression
questions.question_text: Let A be the largest positive integer that divides all the numbers of the form $3^k+4^k+5^k$, and B be the largest positive integer that divides all the numbers of the form $4^k+3(4^k)+4^{k+2}$, where k is any positive integer. Then (A + B) equals
questions.concept:
- When a divisor must work for **every** value of k, test the smallest few values of k and take the GCD of the results.
- If the expression factors cleanly (a common power pulled out), the leftover k-independent part is usually the answer directly — no need to test multiple k.
questions.solution:
1. **Find A by testing small k:** $3^k+4^k+5^k$ gives 12 (k=1), 50 (k=2), 216 (k=3); their GCD is $A=2$.
2. **Simplify B's expression:** $4^k+3(4^k)+4^{k+2}=4^k(1+3+16)=20\times4^k$.
3. **Pull out the k-independent part:** the smallest factor of $4^k$ across all $k\ge1$ is $4^1$, so $B=20\times4=80$.
4. **Add A and B:** $2+80=82$.

*Source: CAT 2022, Slot 1.*

questions.question_text: In a six-digit number, the sixth, that is, the rightmost, digit is the sum of the first three digits, the fifth digit is the sum of first two digits, the third digit is equal to the first digit, the second digit is twice the first digit and the fourth digit is the sum of fifth and sixth digits. Then, the largest possible value of the fourth digit is
questions.concept:
- When later digits are defined in terms of earlier ones, express everything in terms of a single starting variable.
- Chain the relationships forward step by step rather than solving them all at once.
- The "every digit ≤ 9" constraint is usually exactly what pins down the one valid value of your starting variable.
questions.solution:
1. **Name the first digit:** call it $a$.
2. **Chain the other digits from the clues:** digit 2 $=2a$, digit 3 $=a$, digit 5 $=a+2a=3a$, digit 6 $=a+2a+a=4a$.
3. **Compute digit 4:** digit 4 = digit 5 + digit 6 $=3a+4a=7a$.
4. **Cap every digit at 9:** $7a\le9 \Rightarrow a=1$ is the only option.
5. **Read off digit 4:** $7a=7$ (the full number is 121734).

*Source: CAT 2019, Slot 2.*
